records.our_prose: Bok choy flowers (bolts) for two reasons: a cold spell on young plants, more than about a week of nights below 50°F, and summer heat with long days. To avoid it, grow bok choy in the cool parts of the year and lean on the fall crop, plant the spring crop after the hard cold rather than during it, water steadily, and give some afternoon shade when it is warm. Sow a fresh little batch every couple of weeks, pick promptly, and as soon as you see a flower stalk in the middle, harvest the whole plant.

records.our_prose: Bok choy bolts two ways, and both close the eating window. A spell of cold on young plants, more than about a week of nights below 50°F, vernalizes them so they run to seed once it warms (UMN), and separately heat with long days drives a mature plant to flower. Prevent both by growing in the cool shoulders and leaning on the fall crop: sow the spring crop a touch later, after hard cold, rather than rushing it into a cold snap, and time the crop to mature in cool weather. Choose slow-bolting varieties, keep moisture steady, give light afternoon shade in warm spells, and succession sow every 2 weeks so any bolted batch is quickly replaced. Harvest promptly at the first sign of a central seedstalk.

records.our_prose: Bok choy, also called pak choi, is a fast cool-weather Asian green grown for its upright bunch of crisp white or green stalks and tender leaves. It does not form a head like cabbage. It is ready in about a month and grows best in cool weather, and it flowers (bolts) easily from both summer heat and a cold spell on young plants, so the fall crop is the most reliable. Harvest the whole plant, or pick the outer stalks and let it keep growing.

records.our_prose: Your spring planting bolted while still immature, sending up a seedstalk instead of building a rosette. This is vernalization (cold-induced) bolting: a young bok choy plant exposed to a prolonged cold spell, more than about a week of nights below 50°F, is cued to flower once warmth returns (UMN). It is tempting to blame poor seed, but a cold snap on young plants is the usual cause. Next time set the spring crop out a touch later, after the hard cold, shield seedlings from cold snaps with row cover, choose slow-bolting varieties, and lean on the more reliable fall sowing.

records.our_prose: In the low desert bok choy is a fall-through-early-spring crop, and the long summer heat is the off-season, so the bolt trigger that matters here is spring warmth with lengthening days catching a late crop. Sow once the worst summer heat eases in early fall, harvest through winter, and finish before the spring heat ramp, which forces rapid bolting. Watch the other trigger too: a cold snap on very young plants, more than about a week of nights below 50°F, can vernalize them into early flowering, so do not rush the first fall sowing. Harvest the whole plant at the first seedstalk, and do not attempt a summer crop in the low desert.

records.our_prose: On the cool north coast, summer is a fine bok choy season, not one to avoid, because it rarely gets hot enough to make plants bolt from heat. The bolt to watch for here is the cold kind: if young spring plants sit through a cold spell, more than about a week of nights below 50°F, they flower early once it warms, so wait until the hard cold has passed before you sow in spring. Water steadily, and when you see a flower stalk shoot up from the center, harvest the whole plant right away; the leaves stay edible but turn tougher and sharper each day.

records.our_prose: North-coast summers stay mild enough that bok choy runs through them, so the usual summer heat-and-daylength bolt is muted here. The bolt that bites on this coast is the other one: a cold snap on young spring plants, more than about a week of nights below 50°F, vernalizes seedlings into premature flowering, so hold spring sowings until after the hard cold rather than rushing them in. Keep moisture steady, and harvest the whole plant at the first central seedstalk, before the leaf-stalks toughen and sharpen. Unlike inland regions, you do not pause through summer here.

records.our_prose: In Arizona's low desert bok choy is a long cool-season crop from fall through early spring, so the bolt that matters is spring heat: expect bolting as days lengthen and highs climb past the mid-80s°F toward the first 100°F days of early May, and finish the crop before then. Give afternoon shade and even moisture to early-fall and late-winter sowings at the warm edges, where a young plant can also be vernalized into bolting by a long cold snap, more than about a week of nights below 50°F. Harvest the whole plant at the first seedstalk, and do not attempt a summer crop in the low desert.

records.our_prose: In the cold zones bok choy runs as two fast frost-bracketed crops, and the fall sowing is the dependable one. Direct sow or set out small transplants around the last frost, but not into a long cold snap: young bok choy held more than about a week of nights below 50°F bolts once it warms, so the spring window is short and best sown a touch later than the hardiest brassicas. Because the crop matures in roughly 30 to 50 days, the first cutting comes fast, and you can re-sow every couple of weeks until heat ends the spring run. Sow the main crop in mid to late summer to head as nights cool; fall bok choy is sweeter, slower to bolt, and far more reliable than the spring crop. Midsummer is the gap rather than a heat exclusion in the coldest zones, where short nights keep frost, not heat, the limit at both ends.

records.our_prose: Bok choy is best sown straight in the garden because it grows fast and does not like having its roots disturbed, though small transplants work too. Sow the seeds about a quarter to half an inch deep and thin to about 6 inches apart for baby plants or a foot for full-size ones. The big thing to avoid is a cold spell on young plants: more than about a week of nights below 50°F can make them flower (bolt) once it warms up. The fall crop is the most reliable. In hot areas, plant in fall through early spring instead of summer.

records.our_prose: Bok choy is fast and resents root disturbance, so it is often direct sown, though young transplants work well if set out before they become root-bound. Sow seed about 0.25 to 0.5 inch deep (NCSU) and thin to about 6 inches for baby types or 12 to 18 inches for full-size heads (NCSU; UMN). For transplants, start only about 3 weeks ahead and set out small. The timing trap is the cold-snap bolt: bok choy held more than about a week of nights below 50°F bolts once it warms, so avoid setting young spring plants into a long cold spell, and lean on the fall sowing, which is the more reliable crop. In hot regions, shift sowing to fall through early spring, since heat and long days force bolting.
